title: Privacy
paras: Privacy is the condition or claim of an individual or group to be free from unwanted access, observation or disclosure, and to determine for themselves how far they, and information about them, are exposed to others. The concept has no single accepted definition. Lawyers, philosophers and social scientists have variously understood it as a right to be let alone, as limited access to the self, as secrecy, as control over personal information, as a precondition of personhood and intimate relationships, and as the appropriate flow of information within social contexts.

Distinctions between public and private life are found in many ancient societies and religious traditions, but privacy emerged as a distinct legal claim only in the nineteenth century, when new printing and photographic technologies and the popular press prompted calls for legal protection. In the second half of the twentieth century the spread of computers shifted attention from intrusion and publicity towards the collection and processing of personal data, producing a body of data protection law that began in Western Europe in the 1970s and has since spread worldwide.

Privacy is protected as a human right by Article 12 of the Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Article 17 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights and regional instruments such as Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Many national constitutions protect it expressly, and courts in other countries have derived it from broader guarantees. The structure of protection nevertheless differs markedly between jurisdictions: European law tends to treat privacy as an aspect of personal dignity and regulates the processing of personal data comprehensively, whereas law in the United States has traditionally emphasised liberty against the state and regulates the private sector by sector.
